chunks: "The building block is the CMOS inverter: one PMOS from VDD to the output and one NMOS from the output to ground, with both gates tied together as the input.
Input low turns the PMOS on and the NMOS off, so the output is pulled up to VDD. Input high does the opposite and pulls the output to ground.
One of them is always off, so in steady state there's no path from VDD to ground and basically no static current. For a NAND, I extend that.
Two NMOS in series for the pull-down, so the output only goes low when both A and B are high, and two PMOS in parallel for the pull-up, so the output goes high if either input is low.
That's the NAND truth table. A NOR is the dual: NMOS in parallel, PMOS in series.
The general rule is that the pull-down network implements the complement of the function with AND as series and OR as parallel, and the pull-up is its dual.
That's why CMOS gates are naturally inverting, and why an AND gate is really a NAND followed by an inverter, six transistors.
In practice I'd mention sizing: series transistors are weaker, so you make them wider, and the PMOS is wider than the NMOS because holes are slower.
That's also why NAND is preferred over NOR in a library: a NOR has series PMOS, which is the slow type."
